newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina seen cutting 1996 deficit by $1.6 bln.
newsitem.headline: Argentina seen cutting 1996 deficit by $1.6 bln.

text.p: Argentina agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to cut its 1996 fiscal deficit to $5.0 billion from a projected $6.6 billion, a senior government official said.
The $1.6 billion reduction will come from cutbacks in public spending and the increase in revenue from the government's new tax package, Finance Secretary Pablo Guidotti told the daily La Nacion.
The government also agreed with the IMF that 1997 fiscal's shortfall will not exceed $3.0 billion, he said.

The government plans to save $1.0 billion this year from a reduction in pension payments and from the so-called Second Reform of State which is allowing it to streamline operations in the public sector, Guidotti said.
The remaining $600 million will be added revenue from the government's tax package now being discussed in Congress.

Argentina also agreed to suspend planned public works but Guidotti said the money saved there will have to be re-routed to different programs of the social pension system which have incurred in cost overruns.
Visiting Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) President Enrique Iglesias said late Monday that a substantial portion of the country's fiscal deficit will be financed with loans from that bank.
The outlook "opens the way for the IADB to be active in Argentina, with projects that have a large social element of between $2.5 billion and $3.0 billion between 1996 and 1997," said Iglesias.
He added that the Argentine economy "is on the right track and the trend is positive."

On Sunday night, IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said during a brief visit that he had reached a tentative agreement to provide an Extended Fund Facility loan to Argentina and praised government efforts to loosen labor laws and cut the deficit.
"At the end of next week I will be recommending that the IMF board give its blessing to the economic goals," Camdessus said.
He also estimated that economic growth would be five percent next year. Argentina's Economy Ministry expects three percent growth in 1996.
